title: Left calf pain in a 26-year-old on the pill
desc: This station involves a focused calf pain history and lower limb examination of a 26-year-old accountant in general practice, then calculating her Wells score, interpreting her observations, bloods, pregnancy test and venous Doppler ultrasound, diagnosing a provoked proximal deep vein thrombosis, and planning anticoagulation, contraception, follow-up and safety netting.
focus: Unilateral calf pain: VTE risk factors, Wells score, compression ultrasound and outpatient anticoagulation for DVT
stem: You are a medical student on your general practice rotation. Mary Schulz, a 26-year-old woman, has come to see her GP because of pain in her calf. The practice nurse has taken her observations. Your supervising GP has asked you to see Mary first and then present her.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mary and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Mary's observations, her blood results, a urine pregnancy test and a venous ultrasound report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Mary Schulz, a 26-year-old accountant. You are sore and a bit tired from not sleeping well, and you are worried. You limp slightly on your left leg. When the candidate says what they are examining, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "I've had this pain in my calf for a couple of days and it just isn't going away."

The pain (give only when asked):

  • Site: left calf only. It does not spread anywhere.
  • Character: a deep ache.
  • Severity: 7 out of 10.
  • Onset and course: came on gradually 2 days ago and has been there all the time since.
  • Context: "Nothing unusual has happened." You did not hurt it, fall or knock it. Only if asked about sitting, travel or being less active: "I've had to work from home the past few months, so I've just been sitting around all day every day."
  • Aggravating and relieving: you took some Panadol, which helped at first but wore off after a few hours. Walking makes it feel slightly worse.
  • Impact: you are finding it hard to focus on work and to sleep because the pain is there all the time.

Other symptoms (give only if asked about each one):

  • Leg: the calf looks a bit swollen and feels tight and warm. It is maybe a little pinker than the other side, but there is no spreading red patch. No cuts, scratches, insect bites or bruises.
  • Chest: no shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, coughing up blood, racing heart, dizziness or fainting.
  • Infection: no fevers, chills or sweats. You feel well apart from the leg.
  • Knee: no swelling or lump behind the knee before or since the pain started. No knee pain or arthritis.
  • Muscle: no sudden tearing or "being kicked in the calf" feeling, no recent exercise or sport. You can walk on it, just with a limp.
  • Circulation: the pain is not brought on by walking a set distance and then eased by rest. The foot is not pale, cold, numb, tingly or weak.
  • General: no weight loss, night sweats, lumps or change in bowel habit.

Risk factors (only if asked): no recent operation, hospital stay, plaster cast or long flight or car trip. Never had a blood clot. No cancer. You do not smoke.

Periods and pregnancy (only if asked): last period 2 weeks ago, normal and on time; periods are not heavy. You have a boyfriend, take the pill every day and have not missed any. You do not think you could be pregnant.

Bleeding (only if asked): no bleeding problems, easy bruising, stomach ulcers, blood in your poo or wee, or heavy periods. No kidney or liver problems.

Past medical history: acne, anxiety (seeing a psychologist, no tablets) and being overweight. No operations.

Medicines: the oral contraceptive pill ("the normal combined pill", ethinylestradiol with levonorgestrel, for about 5 years) and doxycycline once a day for acne. Panadol over the counter for occasional headaches and for this pain. No supplements. No recreational drugs. No allergies.

Family history: your mother had her gallbladder removed at 57 and has seasonal asthma. Your father is well and has had some skin cancers removed. Your siblings are well. Nobody in the family has had blood clots, as far as you know.

Social history: accountant, working from home for the past few months. Non-smoker. About 2 drinks once a month. You try to walk once a week. You cook some of your own meals and get takeaway the rest of the time. You live at home with your parents, who are supportive, as are your workmates.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: "I'm not sure what it is, I don't remember injuring that area." You are worried it is something serious and that it will affect your ability to walk. You hope to be told what it is and to get something to make it better.

Use plain language. If the candidate uses jargon, say you do not understand. If asked something not in this script, give a realistic answer that does not change the case.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate examines that area)

  • General inspection: comfortable at rest, mild acne on the face, overweight (80 kg, 165 cm, BMI 29.4). Walks with a slight limp on the left. Not short of breath, not pale or sweaty.
  • Vital signs: heart rate 88 beats/min regular, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.2 °C.
  • Inspection of the legs (both exposed and compared): the left calf is visibly swollen compared with the right. Faint diffuse pinkness over the left calf with no clear edge. No skin breaks, ulcers, bruising or insect bites. No visible dilated superficial (collateral) veins. No varicose veins. The thighs look symmetrical.
  • Palpation: the left calf is warmer than the right. Pitting oedema over the left ankle and lower shin; none on the right. Tender along the deep veins in the left calf and in the left popliteal fossa; not tender along the thigh. Right leg normal.
  • Measurements: calf circumference 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity: left 40.0 cm, right 36.5 cm (3.5 cm difference). Thigh circumference 15 cm above the patella equal (54 cm each side), so the whole leg is not swollen.
  • Popliteal fossa and knee: no palpable lump or cyst. Knee normal, no effusion, full range of movement.
  • Calf muscle and Achilles: no palpable defect or bruising in the calf muscle. Thompson (calf squeeze) test normal on both sides.
  • Lymph nodes: no enlarged inguinal lymph nodes. No red streaks up the leg.
  • Vascular: femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses present and equal. Feet warm and pink, capillary refill 2 seconds. Sensation and movement of both feet normal.
  • Homans' sign (if performed): the examiner says "Mild discomfort in the calf."
  • Chest and heart: chest clear, good air entry, no pleural rub. Heart sounds dual, no murmurs, no loud P2. JVP not raised.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self (name and role as a medical student), confirms Mary's identity, gains consent for the examination, offers a chaperone and exposes both legs with dignity.
Uses plain language and open questions, and acknowledges that the pain is affecting her sleep and work and that she is worried about her walking.
History
Characterises the calf pain:

kids.x: Site, radiation, character and severity: left calf only, no radiation, deep ache, 7/10.
Onset and course: gradual onset 2 days ago, constant since.
Aggravating and relieving factors: slightly worse on walking; Panadol helped at first but wore off after a few hours.

check.x: Asks about local features of DVT: calf swelling, warmth and redness.
Asks about symptoms of pulmonary embolism: shortness of breath, chest pain (especially pleuritic), cough, coughing up blood, palpitations, dizziness or fainting.
Explores risk factors for venous thromboembolism:

kids.x: Immobility: elicits months of sitting all day working from home.
Oestrogen: identifies that she takes the combined oral contraceptive pill.
Pregnancy: asks about the last period and the chance of pregnancy.
Others: recent surgery, trauma, hospital stay, plaster cast or long travel; previous clots; family history of clots; active cancer or constitutional symptoms (weight loss, night sweats); smoking.

check.x: Asks targeted questions to rule other causes in or out:
check.d: Credit each kid for at least 2 relevant questions about that cause. Full marks for 3 or more of the 4 kids.

kids.x: Cellulitis: fever or chills, spreading redness, cuts, bites or broken skin as a way in.
Ruptured or dissecting Baker's cyst: swelling or a lump behind the knee before the calf pain, knee arthritis.
Gastrocnemius or soleus tear or bruise: trauma, a sudden tearing feeling during exercise, bruising, difficulty bearing weight.
Peripheral arterial disease or ischaemia: pain on exertion eased by rest, and pallor, coldness, numbness or tingling, or weakness of the foot.

check.x: Asks about bleeding risk before anticoagulation: bleeding problems or easy bruising, heavy periods, stomach ulcers or gut bleeding, and kidney or liver disease.
Takes the past medical history (acne, anxiety, overweight), medicines including over-the-counter, supplements and recreational drugs (pill, doxycycline, Panadol), and allergies (nil).

Takes a family history (no clots; mother cholecystectomy and asthma, father skin cancers) and social history (non-smoker, occasional alcohol, accountant, walks once a week, mixed diet, lives with her parents, supportive parents and workmates).
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations and the impact on her life (does not know the cause, fears it is serious and will affect her walking, struggling to sleep and work).
Examination

Does a general inspection and asks for vital signs (heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature), and examines or states they would examine the chest and heart, looking for signs of pulmonary embolism or infection.
Exposes and compares both legs: swelling, colour and redness, skin breaks, bruising, and dilated superficial (collateral) veins.
Palpates for warmth, pitting oedema and tenderness along the deep veins (calf, popliteal fossa and thigh), comparing with the other leg.
Measures both calf circumferences 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity (3.5 cm difference) and checks whether the whole leg is swollen (thigh circumference equal).
Looks for other causes: feels the popliteal fossa for a cyst and examines the knee; examines the calf muscle and Achilles tendon (Thompson test); checks for red streaks and inguinal lymph nodes.
Examines the arterial supply and neurology: femoral, popliteal and foot pulses, capillary refill, temperature of the feet, sensation and movement.
Interpretation

Calculates the Wells score for DVT and uses it: 3 (tenderness along the deep veins 1, calf swelling more than 3 cm 1, pitting oedema in the symptomatic leg 1, with no alternative diagnosis as likely, so no minus 2) is high probability (0 or less low, 1 to 2 moderate, 3 to 8 high). States this means going straight to compression ultrasound rather than a D-dimer.
check.d: Accept 4 if the candidate counts the immobility (strictly the criterion is bedridden for more than 3 days or major surgery within 4 weeks): it is still high probability.

check.x: Interprets the ultrasound: non-compressible left distal femoral and popliteal veins with thrombus and no flow, extending into the posterior tibial and peroneal veins. This is an acute proximal DVT (the popliteal vein is involved), with no Baker's cyst or muscle haematoma.

Interprets the observations, bloods and pregnancy test: normal and stable observations (no tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypoxia or fever), so no clinical features of PE or sepsis; normal haemoglobin, platelets, kidney and liver function and coagulation, so no barrier to a DOAC; negative urine hCG, so she is not pregnant.

Gives the diagnosis with justification: left proximal DVT, provoked by the combined oral contraceptive pill and prolonged sitting, with excess weight as a further risk factor, and typical symptoms and signs.

Names other causes and why they are less likely: cellulitis (no fever, skin break or spreading redness), claudication (not exertional, normal pulses), ruptured Baker's cyst (no prior swelling behind the knee, none on ultrasound), calf muscle tear or bruise (no trauma or tearing).
Management

Explains in plain words that there is a blood clot in a deep vein of the leg and that blood-thinning medicine stops it growing and lowers the risk of it reaching the lungs while the body clears it. Reassures her that most people walk normally again as the swelling settles, and checks understanding.
Starts anticoagulation today:

kids.x: A DOAC: apixaban 10 mg orally twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily, or rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily with food for 21 days then 20 mg once daily with food.
Or names an acceptable alternative: subcutaneous enoxaparin 1 mg/kg 12-hourly (80 mg for Mary). States warfarin is not used on its own to start treatment.

check.x: States the duration: 3 months for a DVT provoked by a transient risk factor, with a review before stopping.
Addresses contraception and pregnancy:

kids.x: Advises stopping the oestrogen-containing pill because it raises the risk of clotting.
Arranges reliable contraception without oestrogen, ideally a levonorgestrel IUD or the implant (a progestogen-only pill is acceptable; avoid depot injection), and discusses her acne separately.

Explains that blood thinners like apixaban/rivaroxaban are not safe in pregnancy (they cross the placenta and may harm a baby), so she needs reliable contraception and must tell a doctor straight away if she might be pregnant.

check.x: Discusses the plan with the supervising GP. Treats her as an outpatient because she is stable, has no features of PE, has low bleeding risk, has normal bloods and has good support, and refers to ED or the hospital DVT service if any of these change.

Gives practical advice: paracetamol for pain; avoid NSAIDs and aspirin while on anticoagulants; keep walking and break up long periods of sitting; elevate the leg when resting; compression stockings are not routinely needed.
Safety netting
Tells Mary to call 000 for sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing up blood, a racing heart or fainting (possible clot in the lungs).

Tells her to go to ED for signs of serious bleeding on the blood thinner: vomiting blood, black or bloody stools, blood in the urine, very heavy periods, a severe headache, or any head injury. Also to go straight to ED (or call 000) if the leg becomes suddenly much more swollen, very painful, blue or dusky, pale, cold or numb.

Arranges follow-up: GP review within about a week (symptoms, side effects, adherence, contraception), review at 3 months to plan stopping, written information on DVT and her anticoagulant, and telling other doctors, dentists and pharmacists that she is on a blood thinner.

part2.lead: Your supervising GP arranged a same-day venous ultrasound and blood tests. Mary is back from the radiology and pathology practice. Here are her observations, her blood results, the urine pregnancy test done this morning and the ultrasound report.
part2.patient:
Put these questions to the candidate while they explain the plan, if they have not already covered them:

  • "Could the clot go to my lungs?"
  • "Will I be able to walk properly again?"
  • "Do I really have to stop the pill? My skin will get worse."
  • "How long do I have to take the blood thinner for?"

Mary is relieved to have an answer, and calmer once the candidate explains clearly what to watch for.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Taken by the practice nurse, seated, on room air. No observation chart is used in the clinic.
handover.model:
Read: heart rate 88 then 84, blood pressure 124/78 then 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.2 then 37.0 °C, pain 7/10 then 6/10. All values are within normal adult limits and stable across the day. None would trigger a clinical review or rapid response on an adult observation chart.

For Mary: no tachycardia, tachypnoea or hypoxia, so no clinical features of pulmonary embolism. No fever, so cellulitis is less likely.

What it changes: she is stable enough to be treated as an outpatient, and nothing points to a need for CT pulmonary angiography.

rows.note: Practice nurse, seated, before the GP consultation
On return from radiology and pathology

handover.label: Blood tests (collected 11:30 today)
handover.result: Collected before any anticoagulant. D-dimer not requested.
handover.model:
Read: haemoglobin 132 g/L, white cells 7.8 and platelets 268 ×109/L are normal. Kidney function is normal (creatinine 64 µmol/L, eGFR above 90). Liver function tests are normal. INR 1.0 and APTT 29 s are normal.

For Mary: no anaemia, low platelets or clotting problem to raise her bleeding risk, and normal kidney and liver function, so a DOAC can be given at the standard dose. A D-dimer was not needed: with a high Wells score a negative result could not safely exclude DVT, and imaging was going to be done anyway.

What it changes: she can start apixaban or rivaroxaban today. These are also her baseline results for follow-up.

handover.label: Urine pregnancy test (clinic, 09:50)
handover.result: Point-of-care urine test, first-void sample not required. Last menstrual period 2 weeks ago.
handover.model:
Read: urine β-hCG not detected.

For Mary: she is not pregnant (her last period was 2 weeks ago and she takes the pill every day), so pregnancy is not a risk factor here and a DOAC can be used. DOACs are not used in pregnancy, where low molecular weight heparin is the treatment.

What it changes: she can start a DOAC today, but she needs reliable contraception without oestrogen while she is on it, and must tell a doctor at once if she might be pregnant.

handover.label: Venous Doppler ultrasound, left leg
handover.result:
Examination: left lower limb venous duplex ultrasound: whole-leg compression ultrasound with colour and spectral Doppler. Right common femoral vein assessed for comparison.

Clinical details: 26-year-old woman, 2 days of left calf pain and swelling. On the combined oral contraceptive pill. Wells score high.

Findings:

  • Left common femoral vein: fully compressible, normal phasic flow with respiratory variation.
  • Left femoral vein: proximal and mid segments compressible with normal flow. The distal segment (adductor canal) is distended and non-compressible, with echogenic thrombus in the lumen and no colour flow.
  • Left popliteal vein: distended and non-compressible, with occlusive thrombus and no colour or spectral flow.
  • Left calf veins: posterior tibial and peroneal veins non-compressible with thrombus. Gastrocnemius and soleal veins compressible.
  • Superficial veins: left great and small saphenous veins compressible, no thrombus.
  • Popliteal fossa: no Baker's cyst or fluid collection.
  • Calf soft tissues: subcutaneous oedema in the calf. No intramuscular haematoma or muscle tear.
  • Right common femoral vein: compressible, normal phasic flow.

Conclusion: acute occlusive deep vein thrombosis of the left leg, from the distal femoral vein through the popliteal vein into the posterior tibial and peroneal veins. The common femoral vein is clear. No Baker's cyst or muscle injury.
handover.model:
Read: the key sign is non-compressibility of the distal femoral vein, the popliteal vein and the posterior tibial and peroneal veins, with thrombus in the lumen and no flow. The common femoral vein compresses normally. The femoral vein is a deep vein despite its old name, the superficial femoral vein. There is no Baker's cyst, haematoma or muscle tear, so those alternatives are excluded.

For Mary: this is a proximal DVT, because the popliteal vein and above are involved, so it needs anticoagulation, not serial scans. It fits the high Wells score, and it is provoked by the combined pill and months of sitting.

What it changes: start a DOAC today and plan 3 months of treatment. Stop the oestrogen-containing pill and arrange other contraception. Treat her as an outpatient with GP follow-up, safety netting for PE and bleeding, and a review at 3 months.

ask: What was her Wells score from your history and examination, and how did it decide which test to order? What do these results show?
What is the most likely diagnosis, and why? What else did you consider?
What is your management plan: where she is treated, which anticoagulant and dose, for how long, and what about her contraception?
How will you safety-net and follow Mary up?

guide:
In Part 1, give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. Mary mentions working from home only if she is asked about immobility, sitting or activity. If the candidate asks for a D-dimer or an ultrasound in Part 1, say "Your supervisor has arranged tests; you will see the results in Part 2." If they perform Homans' sign, give the finding, but do not give credit for it: it is unreliable, and a calf circumference measurement is what the Wells score uses.

In Part 2, hand over all four results together and ask the questions in order. Mary puts her questions while the candidate explains the plan. For the Wells score (item 22), accept 3 or 4 (if immobility is counted). Both are high probability, and the important step is going to compression ultrasound rather than relying on a D-dimer. The differential diagnosis and Wells score are marked in Part 2, even if the candidate mentions them earlier.

A high-performing candidate characterises the pain and asks about swelling and warmth. They screen for PE, find both the pill and the months of sitting, and ask about pregnancy and bleeding risk. They also ask targeted questions about at least four other causes. Their examination compares both legs, measures the calves 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity, and checks pulses, the popliteal fossa and the chest. In Part 2 they score Wells at 3 (high), read the ultrasound as a proximal DVT, and confirm normal bloods and a negative pregnancy test. They start apixaban or rivaroxaban at the correct loading dose for 3 months and deal with the oestrogen pill and the need for contraception. They treat her as an outpatient with clear red flags for PE and bleeding, and arrange GP follow-up.

A borderline candidate takes a pain history but misses the immobility or the pill, or does not ask about PE symptoms or pregnancy. They may order a D-dimer and stop there, call the popliteal clot "distal", or start warfarin alone. They may leave her on the combined pill, or close with "come back if it gets worse".
explain:
The diagnosis: provoked proximal DVT

Mary has 2 days of gradual, constant, aching left calf pain with swelling and warmth, worse on walking. She has two clear provoking factors: an oestrogen-containing combined oral contraceptive pill and months of sitting all day while working from home. Being overweight adds to the risk. On examination she has tenderness along the deep veins, a 3.5 cm difference in calf circumference and unilateral pitting oedema. The ultrasound confirms an occlusive thrombus from the distal femoral vein through the popliteal vein into the calf veins. This is a proximal DVT, because it involves the popliteal vein or veins above it. DVT can be asymptomatic, and it can also cause pain, swelling, redness and warmth, usually in one leg but sometimes both.

Risk factors for venous thromboembolism

Immobility or a long hospital stay; recent surgery or trauma; obesity; previous VTE; cancer, or constitutional symptoms that suggest it; oral contraceptives or HRT; pregnancy or the postpartum period; stroke with hemiplegia or immobility; age over 65; family history of VTE; heart failure; and inflammatory bowel disease.

The Wells score for DVT and the testing pathway

CriterionPointsMary
Paralysis, paresis or recent plaster cast of a leg10
Recently bedridden for more than 3 days, or major surgery within 4 weeks10
Localised tenderness along the deep venous system11
Entire leg swollen10
Calf swelling more than 3 cm compared with the other leg (10 cm below the tibial tuberosity)11
Pitting oedema greater in the symptomatic leg11
Collateral superficial veins (not varicose)10
Active cancer, or treatment within 6 months10
Alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT−20

A score of 0 or less is low probability, 1 to 2 moderate and 3 to 8 high. Mary scores 3, which is high. Low or moderate probability: do a D-dimer first, and a negative result makes DVT unlikely. High probability: go straight to compression ultrasound (proximal or whole-leg), because a negative D-dimer cannot safely exclude DVT. If the ultrasound cannot be done promptly in someone with a high probability and no contraindication, anticoagulation is usually started while waiting. Working from home is a real risk factor, but it does not meet the strict "bedridden" criterion. Homans' sign is unreliable and should not be used.

Compression ultrasound

Compression ultrasound with Doppler is the test of choice. The diagnostic sign is a vein that cannot be compressed by the probe, often with visible thrombus and no colour flow. The report also excludes the alternatives here: no Baker's cyst, no muscle haematoma and clear superficial veins.

Differentials

  • Cellulitis: pain, swelling, redness and warmth, often with fever and a way in for infection (a cut, bite or bruise). Mary has no fever and no skin break, and the pinkness is faint and diffuse.
  • Peripheral arterial disease or acute limb ischaemia: exertional pain eased by rest, or the 6 Ps (pain, pallor, paraesthesia, perishingly cold, pulselessness, paralysis). Her pulses are normal and her foot is warm.
  • Ruptured or dissecting Baker's cyst: swelling behind the knee before the calf pain, and it can closely mimic DVT. She had no prior swelling, and none was seen on ultrasound.
  • Gastrocnemius or soleus tear or bruise: a sudden tearing feeling during exercise, bruising and difficulty bearing weight. She had no trauma or exercise, and the scan shows no haematoma.

Interpreting the other results

Her observations are normal and stable, so there are no clinical features of PE. Her blood count, kidney and liver function and coagulation are normal, so there is no barrier to standard-dose DOAC treatment. The negative pregnancy test matters because DOACs are not used in pregnancy, where low molecular weight heparin is used instead.

Management

  • Anticoagulation is the treatment. The choice depends on where the clot is and on the bleeding risk. Options include an oral factor Xa inhibitor, a low molecular weight heparin, fondaparinux or unfractionated heparin. Warfarin is not appropriate on its own to start treatment.
    • Apixaban 10 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily.
    • Rivaroxaban 15 mg orally twice daily with food for 21 days, then 20 mg once daily with food.
    • Alternative: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously 12-hourly.
  • Duration: 3 months for a proximal DVT provoked by a transient risk factor, then review. Longer treatment is considered for unprovoked or recurrent VTE or persistent risk factors.
  • Contraception: oestrogen raises the risk of clotting, so the combined pill should be stopped and replaced with a method without oestrogen. Reliable contraception is essential while she is on a DOAC, because DOACs cross the placenta, there are not enough safety data and they are contraindicated in pregnancy. The preferred options are a levonorgestrel IUD, which also reduces the heavier periods that anticoagulants can cause, or the implant. A progestogen-only pill is acceptable. The depot medroxyprogesterone injection is usually avoided after VTE, and a copper IUD can make periods heavier. Her acne needs a separate plan.
  • Setting: a stable patient with DVT and no features of PE, low bleeding risk, normal bloods and good support can be treated as an outpatient in general practice. Otherwise refer to ED or a hospital DVT service.
  • Symptoms and activity: paracetamol for pain; avoid NSAIDs and aspirin, which add to the bleeding risk; keep walking and break up long periods of sitting; elevate the leg at rest. Compression stockings are not routinely recommended to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome, but may help symptoms.
  • Further testing: for a provoked DVT with no suspicious features, thrombophilia testing and extensive cancer screening are not routinely needed. A careful history, examination and basic bloods are enough.

Safety netting and follow-up

Call 000 for sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing up blood, a racing heart or fainting. Go to ED for major bleeding (vomiting blood, black or bloody stools, blood in the urine, very heavy periods, a severe headache or any head injury) or for a leg that suddenly becomes much more swollen, blue, pale, cold or numb. Arrange GP review within about a week to check symptoms, side effects, adherence and contraception, and a 3-month review to plan stopping treatment. Give written information, and ask her to tell every prescriber, dentist and pharmacist that she is taking an anticoagulant.
points: In unilateral calf pain, ask specifically about immobility, oestrogen (the pill or HRT) and pregnancy, and screen for PE: risk factors are often only mentioned when asked about.
Wells score for DVT: 0 or less low, 1 to 2 moderate, 3 to 8 high. Low or moderate probability gets a D-dimer; high probability goes straight to compression ultrasound.
Measure both calves 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity: a difference of more than 3 cm is a Wells criterion. Homans' sign is unreliable.
The diagnostic ultrasound sign is a vein that cannot be compressed. A clot in the popliteal vein or above is a proximal DVT and needs anticoagulation.

Start a DOAC at the loading dose (apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, or rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days). Treat a DVT provoked by a transient risk factor for 3 months. Warfarin is never used on its own to start treatment.

Stop oestrogen-containing contraception and arrange a reliable alternative (ideally a levonorgestrel IUD or the implant), because DOACs are not safe in pregnancy: they cross the placenta and may harm a baby. Safety-net for PE (000) and bleeding (ED).
